concepts.title: Nation and Nationalism: Defining the Political Community

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nation and Nationalism: Defining the Political Community' refers to.
questions.a: A nation is a community of people who feel bound to one another by shared identity -- history, culture, territory, or aspirations -- and who believe they should govern themselves together. Nationalism is the sentiment and the political doctrine that this collective self-rule matters, demanding that nation and state coincide.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nation and Nationalism: Defining the Political Community'.
questions.a: Nations are made, not found -- a shared sense of peoplehood built on memory, culture and common aspirations.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nation and Nationalism: Defining the Political Community' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps107.txt lines 1-90 (overview and introduction, meaning of nation and nationalism, nation as community with shared identity and aspirations))

concepts.title: Assumptions of Nationalism: Shared Beliefs and Collective Identity

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Assumptions of Nationalism: Shared Beliefs and Collective Identity' refers to.
questions.a: National self-rule rests on shared beliefs: that history is one common story, that territory is one collective home, that political ideals and cultural traits bind members, and that the community's destiny matters more than internal differences. Nationalists read a single past and project a single future for the whole people.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Assumptions of Nationalism: Shared Beliefs and Collective Identity'.
questions.a: One land, one story, one future -- these shared beliefs manufacture the collective 'we'.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Assumptions of Nationalism: Shared Beliefs and Collective Identity' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps107.txt lines 90-170 (shared beliefs underlying nationalism, common history, territory, shared political ideals, common culture))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Self-Determination and National Movements' refers to.
questions.a: Nationalism claims the right of every nation to decide its own political fate -- self-determination. This principle fuelled anti-colonial movements, redrew European maps, and still drives stateless nations seeking statehood, raising hard questions about where one nation's freedom ends and another's begins.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Self-Determination and National Movements'.
questions.a: Every people its own master -- the powerful, dangerous simplicity of self-determination.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Self-Determination and National Movements' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps107.txt lines 170-260 (national self-determination, nineteenth century Europe, anti-colonial movements, first and second world war context))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nationalism: Inclusive and Exclusive Faces' refers to.
questions.a: Nationalism can bind citizens across caste and creed in solidarity and inspire democratic self-rule, yet it can also harden into suspicion of outsiders and suppression of internal diversity. Whether it unites or persecutes depends on whether national identity stays open to pluralism or demands uniformity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nationalism: Inclusive and Exclusive Faces'.
questions.a: Same force, two faces -- nationalism builds solidarity when plural, turns exclusionary when uniform.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nationalism: Inclusive and Exclusive Faces' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: keps107.txt lines 260-350 (positive and negative dimensions of nationalism, pluralism, cultural diversity, dangers of aggressive nationalism))
